T1: Health‑conscious consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyser if they perceive it as a reliable, easy‑to‑use tool for personal health monitoring, and Tanita can capture value by selling premium, branded devices directly to consumers. Who benefits: Individual health‑conscious consumers seeking accurate body‑composition data for personal health management.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers trust medical evidence linking excess body fat to chronic diseases; they seek measurable, actionable health data; and a trusted brand like Tanita signals accuracy and reliability.. How value is captured: Tanita sells directly to consumers at premium prices, leveraging its existing brand reputation for precision; it also offers subscription services for data tracking and updates.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a branded, clinically validated device.; Tanita can produce a consumer‑friendly version of its stand‑on analyser at a price point acceptable to home users.; Distribution channels (retail, online) are accessible to Tanita.. Predictions: In a test offering the device to 1,000 health‑conscious households, at least 30% will purchase within 12 weeks.; Purchase intent will be higher when presented with medical evidence linking body fat to health risks compared to a generic health‑tracking device.; Repeat purchase rate for subscription services will exceed 20% among existing users..

T2: Health‑conscious consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyser if they perceive it as a status symbol and a way to demonstrate personal health commitment, and Tanita can capture value by positioning the device as a premium, lifestyle product sold through specialty retailers and direct‑to‑consumer channels. Who benefits: Individual health‑conscious consumers seeking to signal wellness and differentiate themselves from peers.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers use health data as a social signal of achievement and commitment; a branded, high‑end device becomes a visible marker of personal health dedication.. How value is captured: Tanita sells through design‑focused retailers and online marketplaces at premium prices, leveraging the device’s aesthetic appeal and brand prestige to command higher margins.. Assumptions: Consumers associate health data with social status and are willing to pay for visible health credentials.; Tanita can design a consumer‑friendly version that is aesthetically appealing and easy to use.; Specialty retailers and online marketplaces will stock a premium health device.. Predictions: In a test offering the device to 1,000 health‑conscious consumers via design‑focused retailers, at least 20% will purchase within 12 weeks.; Purchase intent will be higher when the device is presented as a status symbol rather than a purely functional health tool.; Repeat purchase rate for accessories or upgrades will exceed 15% among existing users..

Test "Musician vs Outdoor User Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Participants view two hypothetical Hellberg earplugs: a high-fidelity version for musicians (no impact on sound) and a lightweight, earplug-integrated headband for outdoor users (no bulk). They indicate which they would buy, the price they would pay, and the likelihood they would use it regularly. The test also captures demographic and current earplug use.. Sample: 200 participants: 100 self-identified early-career musicians (aged 18-35, active in music) and 100 outdoor enthusiasts (aged 18-45, engage in activities like hiking, cycling, skiing). Recruited via panel to match demographic distribution.. Measure: Primary outcome: proportion of musicians who select the high-fidelity version (indicating willingness to adopt) and proportion of outdoor enthusiasts who select the integrated version (indicating willingness to adopt). Secondary: average WTP for each segment.. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of musicians will select the high-fidelity version at a price 1.5x standard earplugs, indicating demand for sound fidelity.; T2: At least 25% of outdoor enthusiasts will select the integrated version at a price 1.2x standard earplugs, indicating demand for comfort and integration.. Decision rule: If musicians select the high-fidelity version at ≥30% and outdoor enthusiasts select the integrated version at ≥25%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting the respective segment. If only one segment meets its threshold, focus on that segment. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on existing B2B/industrial customers and the current consumer offering. Run the proposed choice-based conjoint survey (Test X1) to empirically test demand for a high-fidelity musician proposition and a lightweight outdoor proposition before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment. Who benefits: Households with small gardens and limited storage space who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.. How value is captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.. Assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.; Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.; Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.. Predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.; Surveyed willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose tractor will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable single‑purpose model..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a status symbol and status-driven purchase, because they associate the tractor with modern, affluent lifestyle and community recognition. Who benefits: Affluent households and early adopters who use lawn care as a way to signal social status and modern living.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers seek products that convey prestige and align with their social circle. A tractor that is marketed as a stylish, innovative tool becomes a visible marker of affluence.. How value is captured: Deere can price the tractor at a premium, sell branded apparel and accessories, and build a community around ownership, creating a lifestyle brand that commands higher margins.. Assumptions: Status is a primary purchase driver for a segment of small‑holder households.; Modern, aesthetically pleasing design is valued over purely functional features.; Deere can design a tractor that is visually distinctive without compromising performance.. Predictions: In a test offering a status‑oriented tractor at a price above comparable functional models, purchase intent among affluent respondents will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a purely functional tractor.; Willingness to pay for a status‑oriented tractor will be at least 15% higher than for a comparable functional model..

Test "Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractor" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a differentiated lawn and garden tractor (multi‑purpose vs status‑oriented). They are asked about willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (binary: would buy or not). The survey also captures demographic information (income, homeownership status, self‑identified lifestyle).. Sample: 500 U.S. adults who have a small garden and own a home (estimated from 2020 census data). Recruitment via an online panel to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: 1) Average willingness to pay (EUR) for each tractor variant. 2) Percentage of participants with purchase intent (would buy) for each variant.. Predictions: T1: Multi‑purpose tractor will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than status‑oriented tractor because consumers value versatility and affordability.; T2: Status‑oriented tractor will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than multi‑purpose tractor because consumers value prestige and modern lifestyle.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the multi‑purpose tractor exceeds that of the status‑oriented tractor by at least 10% (e.g., €200 vs €180), we conclude T1 is more likely. If the status‑oriented tractor exceeds by at least 10%, we conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is <10%,. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on the existing B2B dealer network and existing product lines. Conduct a limited pilot test of a multi‑purpose lawn and garden tractor to validate demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on the existing B2B dealer network and existing product lines. Conduct a limited pilot test of a multi‑purpose lawn and garden tractor to validate demand before scaling. Value proposition: A compact, multi‑purpose lawn and garden tractor that performs several tasks (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) without compromising durability, offering affordability and practicality.. The pilot test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the pilot shows purchase intent for the multi‑purpose tractor at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor, and average willingness to pay at least 10% higher, we would proceed to develop a differentiated model.; If the pilot shows no significant difference or negative results, we would maintain focus on the existing B2B business.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment. Who benefits: Households with small gardens and limited storage space who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.. How value is captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.. Assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.; Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.; Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.. Predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.; Surveyed willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose tractor will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable single‑purpose model..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a status symbol and status-driven purchase, because they associate the tractor with modern, affluent lifestyle and community recognition. Who benefits: Affluent households and early adopters who use lawn care as a way to signal social status and modern living.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers seek products that convey prestige and align with their social circle. A tractor that is marketed as a stylish, innovative tool becomes a visible marker of affluence.. How value is captured: Deere can price the tractor at a premium, sell branded apparel and accessories, and build a community around ownership, creating a lifestyle brand that commands higher margins.. Assumptions: Status is a primary purchase driver for a segment of small‑holder households.; Modern, aesthetically pleasing design is valued over purely functional features.; Deere can design a tractor that is visually distinctive without compromising performance.. Predictions: In a test offering a status‑oriented tractor at a price above comparable functional models, purchase intent among affluent respondents will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a purely functional tractor.; Willingness to pay for a status‑oriented tractor will be at least 15% higher than for a comparable functional model..

Test "Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractor" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized product presentation. Participants view a mock 1962 lawn and garden tractor described as a versatile, low‑cost tool for multiple yard tasks. Half see a functional description emphasizing affordability and practicality; half see a status‑oriented description emphasizing modern design, prestige, and community signaling. After viewing, participants indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point. Sample: 200 U.S. households with small gardens (under 0.5 acres) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and region.. Measure: Mean WTP in euros for each version. Secondary measure: purchase intent (binary: would buy within 6 months).. Predictions: T1: Mean WTP for the functional version will be at least 10% higher than for the status version.; T2: Mean WTP for the status version will be at least 10% higher than for the functional version.. Decision rule: If functional WTP ≥ status WTP + 10% → adopt T1; else if status WTP ≥ functional WTP + 10% → adopt T2; else inconclusive.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on the existing B2B dealer network and existing product lines. Conduct a limited pilot test of a functional, low‑cost multi‑purpose tractor to validate demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Target customer: Small‑holder households with limited storage and budget, who need a versatile tool for multiple yard tasks.. Value proposition: A compact, affordable lawn and garden tractor that performs multiple tasks, reducing tool count and simplifying maintenance, while leveraging Deere’s tractor engineering.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (200 participants, 6 weeks, €8,000) to measure willingness to pay for a functional vs. status‑oriented tractor. Use results to decide whether to proceed with a limited pilot or abandon consumer. Uncertainty: Demand for a differentiated consumer product is uncertain due to lack of direct evidence of purchase intent or willingness to pay. The evidence base shows a rapidly growing market for garden tractors but does not confirm that consumers will. Would change if: If the survey shows functional willingness to pay at least 10% higher than status, we would shift to favor T1 and pursue a pilot. If status willingness to pay dominates, we would reconsider a premium; If new evidence from 1960‑62 shows clear consumer adoption of a differentiated model, we would accelerate development.; If independent market research from the era confirms that status was a primary purchase driver, we would shift focus to a status‑oriented proposition.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Who benefits: Households with small gardens and limited storage space who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. How value is captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling the GyPSI 406 PLB directly to consumers through retail channels, charging a premium for a trusted, FCC-approved device.. events.text: Objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must address the specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, emergency preparedness, or a niche market) and not general market trends.. Who benefits: Outdoor recreation users (hikers, campers, paddlers) and their families who rely on emergency response.. Why behaviour changes: Legal approval and mandatory registration create a perceived safety benefit; users trust a device that can be detected by SAR teams, reducing anxiety and encouraging purchase.. How value is captured: ACR can charge a premium for a certified, easy-to-use PLB, sell through outdoor retailers, and potentially bundle with safety courses or insurance, capturing higher margins than generic PLBs.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in the U.S. is large enough to support a differentiated product.; Users are willing to pay more for a device that improves survival chances.; Distribution channels (outdoor retailers) are accessible to ACR.. Predictions: In a test offering the PLB to outdoor recreation groups, purchase intent will be higher than for a generic PLB at the same price.; Surveyed users will cite reduced search time and improved SAR detection as primary purchase drivers..

Why behaviour changes: Legal approval and mandatory registration create a tangible safety product; consumers trust a device that can be detected by SAR teams, reducing anxiety and encouraging purchase.. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a practical, low‑cost tool for multiple tasks, because they value versatility and ease of use over specialized equipment. Who benefits: Households with small gardens and limited storage space who need a versatile tool for various yard tasks.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently use multiple tools (e.g., lawnmower, tiller, snow blower) and find them cumbersome. A single, compact tractor that can perform several tasks reduces tool count and simplifies maintenance.. How value is captured: Deere can charge a premium for a multi‑purpose tractor, sell accessories and attachments, and build brand loyalty among small‑holders who appreciate a single, reliable machine.. Assumptions: Small‑holder households have limited budget for multiple specialized tools.; Versatility is a primary purchase criterion for these consumers.; Deere can engineer a compact tractor that performs multiple tasks without compromising durability.. Predictions: In a test offering a multi‑purpose tractor at a price comparable to a single‑purpose lawnmower, purchase intent among small‑holder respondents will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for a single‑purpose tractor.; Surveyed willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose tractor will be at least 10% higher than for a comparable single‑purpose model..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated lawn and garden tractor if they perceive it as a status symbol and status-driven purchase, because they associate the tractor with modern, affluent lifestyle and community recognition. Who benefits: Affluent households and early adopters who use lawn care as a way to signal social status and modern living.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers seek products that convey prestige and align with their social circle. A tractor that is marketed as a stylish, innovative tool becomes a visible marker of affluence.. How value is captured: Deere can price the tractor at a premium, sell branded apparel and accessories, and build a community around ownership, creating a lifestyle brand that commands higher margins.. Assumptions: Status is a primary purchase driver for a segment of small‑holder households.; Modern, aesthetically pleasing design is valued over purely functional features.; Deere can design a tractor that is visually distinctive without compromising performance.. Predictions: In a test offering a status‑oriented tractor at a price above comparable functional models, purchase intent among affluent respondents will be at least 10 percentage points higher than for a purely functional tractor.; Willingness to pay for a status‑oriented tractor will be at least 15% higher than for a comparable functional model..

T1: Residential boat owners will adopt Jotun marine coatings if they perceive the brand as premium and reliable, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases. Who benefits: Jotun gains premium pricing and brand loyalty from DIY and residential boat owners.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from generic marine paints to Jotun when they associate the brand with superior durability, safety, and environmental compliance, especially after learning about biofouling regulations.. How value is captured: Jotun can charge a premium price for marine coatings and sell through existing distribution channels (e.g., Jotun Multicolor Centers) without major new channels.. Assumptions: Residential boat owners are willing to pay more for perceived quality and safety.; Biofouling regulations increase awareness of paint performance.; Jotun's existing distribution can reach residential buyers.. Predictions: Surveyed residential boat owners will indicate Jotun as their preferred marine paint when asked about quality and safety.; Willingness-to-pay studies will show a price premium of at least 10% over generic marine paints.; Repeat purchase rate for Jotun coatings will be higher than for competitors among DIY users..

T2: Residential boat owners will adopt Jotun marine coatings if they receive personalized recommendations from DIY experts or online forums, because trust in expert advice drives purchase decisions. Who benefits: Jotun gains higher conversion rates and repeat purchases from DIY users who follow expert recommendations.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers rely on expert opinions to validate product performance and safety; when experts recommend Jotun, they are more likely to try it.. How value is captured: Jotun can increase sales through existing distribution by leveraging expert endorsements and online communities, without major new marketing spend.. Assumptions: DIY experts and online forums influence residential boat purchase decisions.; Jotun's coatings are discussed and recommended by these channels.; Consumers trust expert advice more than brand messaging.. Predictions: Surveyed DIY users will report that expert recommendations were a key factor in choosing Jotun.; Web traffic from DIY forums to Jotun's website will increase when featuring expert reviews.; Purchase conversion rate among users exposed to expert recommendations will be at least 15% higher than baseline..

Test "Residential Boat Owner Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a premium brand message (emphasizing Jotun’s marine coatings as premium, reliable, and compliant with biofouling regulations) or an expert recommendation message (stating that DIY experts recommend Jotun for superior performance and safety). Participants are residential boat owners who have owned a boat for at least 2 years and have purchased marine coatings in the past 3 years. They are recruited via an online panel to. Sample: 300 residential boat owners (150 per condition) recruited from Norway, Sweden, and Denmark, balanced by boat ownership duration and prior marine coating purchase.. Measure: Primary outcome: willingness to pay (WTP) premium over a generic marine paint. Secondary outcomes: purchase intent (binary: “Would buy Jotun within 6 months”) and perceived importance of biofouling compliance.. Predictions: T1: Participants exposed to the premium brand message will show a WTP premium of at least 10% over a generic marine paint and higher purchase intent than those exposed to the expert recommendation message.; T2: Participants exposed to the expert recommendation message will show a WTP premium of at least 10% over a generic marine paint and higher purchase intent than those exposed to the premium brand message.. Decision rule: If the difference in average WTP between the premium and expert conditions exceeds 5% (e.g., premium WTP ≥ 105% of generic, expert WTP ≤ 95% of generic), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium branding. If the difference is <5%,. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on B2B marine, protective, and powder coatings. Run the proposed residential boat owner purchase intent test (X1) to empirically compare premium branding versus expert recommendation messaging before any expansion. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer purchase drivers for marine coatings. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on B2B marine, protective, and powder coatings. Run the proposed residential boat owner purchase intent test (X1) to empirically compare premium branding versus expert recommendation messaging before any expansion. Target customer: Residential boat owners (DIY and professional boat owners who purchase marine coatings for their boats).. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition would emphasize Jotun’s marine coatings as premium, reliable, and compliant with biofouling regulations, potentially commanding a price premium and leveraging existing distribution channels.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the residential boat owner purchase intent test (X1) within the 12‑week timeframe and budget of €18,000.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources published before mid-2024; no internal company data is available. Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer purchase data.. Would change if: If the test shows a WTP premium of at least 10% over a generic marine paint and higher purchase intent for the premium brand message, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium branding.; If the test shows a WTP premium of at least 10% for the expert recommendation message, we would consider a co‑branding or licensing model leveraging expert endorsements.; If the test shows no significant premium or no difference between conditions, we would recommend retaining B2B focus and not proceeding with consumer expansion.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Musicians will adopt premium hearing protection if it does not impede listening and performance, because they value clear sound and safety. Who benefits: Musicians and early‑career musicians who need reliable hearing protection without compromising auditory experience.. Why behaviour changes: If a product meets both safety requirements and preserves listening quality, musicians will switch from generic earplugs to a differentiated brand.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium price for models that meet performance criteria, and build brand reputation as the preferred choice for musicians.. Assumptions: Musicians are willing to pay more for products that do not affect sound quality.; Performance‑critical use cases (live performances, practice) drive purchase decisions.; Brand reputation for musical performance compatibility can be leveraged across segments.. Predictions: In a test offering a performance‑optimized model at a premium price, at least 30% of target musicians will purchase within 12 weeks.; Purchase intent will be higher among musicians who report current use of generic earplugs and express dissatisfaction with sound quality..

T2: Outdoor enthusiasts will adopt premium hearing protection if it is lightweight, comfortable, and integrates with outdoor gear, because they value portability and compatibility with activities. Who benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, cyclists) who need hearing protection that does not restrict movement or interfere with gear.. Why behaviour changes: If a product meets both comfort and integration criteria, users will switch from generic earplugs to a differentiated brand that aligns with their outdoor lifestyle.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price models for outdoor use at a premium, and sell through outdoor retailers and specialty channels, leveraging its existing distribution network.. Assumptions: Outdoor users prioritize comfort and compatibility over cost.; Integration with existing gear (e.g., helmets, backpacks) is a key purchase driver.; Brand reputation for outdoor compatibility can be leveraged across segments.. Predictions: In a test offering a lightweight, integrated model at a premium price, at least 25% of target outdoor enthusiasts will purchase within 12 weeks.; Purchase intent will be higher among users who report current use of generic earplugs and express frustration with bulkiness..

Test "Performance vs Comfort Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey experiment with targeted recruitment of two distinct segments: musicians and outdoor enthusiasts. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two product descriptions: (A) Performance-optimized model emphasizing sound quality and safety for musicians; (B) Lightweight, integrated model emphasizing comfort and compatibility for outdoor enthusiasts. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 0‑10 scale and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 200 participants: 100 musicians (recruited via music forums and schools) and 100 outdoor enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor activity forums and hiking clubs). Stratified to ensure balanced representation across age and experience levels.. Measure: Purchase intent score (0‑10) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Musicians exposed to performance description will report higher purchase intent and higher price than those exposed to comfort description.; T2: Outdoor enthusiasts exposed to comfort description will report higher purchase intent and higher price than those exposed to performance description.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for musicians exposed to performance description exceeds the average for outdoor enthusiasts exposed to comfort description by at least 1.5 points on the 0‑10 scale, proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition targeting musicians. If the. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on existing B2B/industrial customers and the current consumer offering. Run the proposed Performance vs Comfort Messaging Test to empirically compare purchase intent for musicians versus outdoor enthusiasts before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse efficiency and does not address consumer demand, performance barriers, or willingness to pay for premium hearing protection. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on existing B2B/industrial customers and the current consumer offering. Run the proposed Performance vs Comfort Messaging Test to empirically compare purchase intent for musicians versus outdoor enthusiasts before committing resources. Target customer: Musicians and early‑career musicians who need reliable hearing protection without compromising auditory experience, and outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, cyclists) who need hearing protection that does not restrict movement or interfere. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that either meets performance barriers for musicians (premium, sound‑preserving models) or integrates comfort and outdoor compatibility for outdoor enthusiasts (lightweight, integrated models).. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the Performance vs Comfort Messaging Test (200 participants, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for each segment.. Uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage. The test will resolve whether musicians or outdoor enthusiasts show higher intent for their respective product. Would change if: If the test shows musicians exposed to performance messaging achieve purchase intent at least 1.5 points higher than outdoor enthusiasts exposed to comfort messaging, proceed to develop a performance‑focused consumer line.; If the test shows outdoor enthusiasts exposed to comfort messaging achieve purchase intent at least 1.5 points higher than musicians exposed to performance messaging, proceed to develop an integrated outdoor line.; If neither segment shows sufficient intent or willingness to pay, abandon the consumer expansion and maintain the current B2B focus.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Hellberg Safety should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current hearing-protection offering, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must consider current reach to individual buyers (unknown from brief).; Investment must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, outdoor enthusiasts).; 2) Expand the existing hearing‑protection line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., fashion‑oriented earplugs, premium branding).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing B2B/industrial customers and current consumer offering without new consumer propositions.; 4) License Hellberg technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than creating a direct consumer proposition..

T1: Musicians will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it does not impede listening and performing, because they currently avoid standard earplugs due to sound distortion. Who benefits: Musicians who need to hear their performances and audience clearly.. Why behaviour changes: If a product reduces sound distortion while still providing adequate protection, musicians will switch from avoiding earplugs to actively using them.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium for models that preserve sound quality, and can sell directly to musicians via online channels.. Assumptions: Musicians are willing to pay more for a product that does not compromise sound quality.; There is sufficient awareness of Hellberg among musicians to reach them directly.; The product can be produced at a price point that justifies a premium.. Predictions: In a test offering two versions of Hellberg earplugs (standard vs. sound-preserving), musicians will choose the sound-preserving version at a higher rate than the standard version.; Purchase intent will be higher among musicians who report sound distortion as a barrier to using earplugs..

T2: Outdoor enthusiasts will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it is lightweight, comfortable, and seamlessly integrates with outdoor gear, because they currently avoid earplugs due to bulk and lack of compatibility with activities. Who benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts who need protection without compromising mobility or gear integration.. Why behaviour changes: If a product is designed for outdoor use (e.g., waterproof, lightweight, compatible with helmets/headlamps), users will switch from not using earplugs to actively wearing them during activities.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price a premium outdoor-specific model and sell through outdoor retailers and direct-to-consumer channels, capturing value through volume sales and brand extension.. Assumptions: Outdoor enthusiasts are willing to pay more for a product that does not restrict movement or compatibility.; There is sufficient market awareness of Hellberg among outdoor users to reach them.; The product can be produced at a price point that justifies a premium for outdoor features.. Predictions: In a test offering two versions of Hellberg earplugs (standard vs. outdoor-specific), outdoor enthusiasts will choose the outdoor-specific version at a higher rate than the standard version.; Purchase intent will be higher among outdoor enthusiasts who report bulk/compatibility as a barrier to using earplugs..

Test "Musician vs Outdoor Consumer Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 200 respondents: 100 self-identified musicians (recruited via music forums and social media) and 100 outdoor enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor activity forums and social media).. Measure: 1) Choice: respondents view two versions of a Hellberg earplug prototype: Standard (no sound preservation) and Sound-Preserving (uses proprietary technology to reduce distortion while maintaining protection). They select which version they would buy. 2) WTP: respondents state the maximum price they would pay for each version (in euros).. Predictions: T1: Musicians will choose the Sound-Preserving version at a rate ≥55% and will report a WTP ≥ €30 for it, indicating they value sound preservation over standard protection.; T2: Outdoor enthusiasts will choose the Sound-Preserving version at a rate <40% and will report a WTP < €25 for it, indicating they prioritize comfort/bulk over sound preservation.. Decision rule: If the observed choice rate for the Sound-Preserving version among musicians is ≥55% AND the average WTP for musicians is ≥ €30, proceed with developing a differentiated musician proposition. If the observed choice rate for the Sound-Preserving version among outdoor enthusiasts is <40% AND the average WTP for outdoor enthusiasts is < €25, proceed with developing a differentiated outdoor proposition. If neither. Cost: 12000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, run the proposed choice-based conjoint survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether musicians would adopt a sound-preserving version and whether outdoor enthusiasts would adopt an outdoor-specific version. The test will determine whether there is sufficient demand and willingness to pay for each segment before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-B shows that a softer, better-fitting protector did not increase wear frequency compared to a standard one. This does not address whether musicians would switch to a sound-preserving version, nor does it quantify willingness to pay. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-B.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, run the proposed choice-based conjoint survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether musicians would adopt a sound-preserving version and whether outdoor enthusiasts would adopt an outdoor-specific version. The test will determine whether there is sufficient demand and willingness to pay for each segment before committing resources. Target customer: Musicians (for sound-preserving proposition) and outdoor enthusiasts (for outdoor-specific proposition). Value proposition: A differentiated Hellberg earplug that either preserves sound quality for musicians or integrates seamlessly with outdoor gear for enthusiasts, positioned as a premium product with willingness to pay tested before launch.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute Test X1 within the €12,000 budget and 10‑week timeline, recruiting 200 respondents (100 musicians and 100 outdoor enthusiasts) and measuring choice and willingness-to-pay for the sound-preserving version.. Uncertainty: Demand for a sound-preserving version among musicians and willingness to pay €30+; demand for an outdoor-specific version among outdoor enthusiasts and willingness to pay €25+; overall market size and competitive landscape for each segment.. Would change if: If the choice rate for the sound-preserving version among musicians is ≥55% and the average willingness-to-pay is ≥€30, proceed with developing a musician-focused proposition.; If the choice rate for the outdoor-specific version among outdoor enthusiasts is ≥40% and the average willingness-to-pay is ≥€25, proceed with developing an outdoor-focused proposition.; If neither segment meets its respective thresholds, reconsider expansion or license the technology to third‑party brands.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.
